The Seahorse is driven by an internal combustion engine, giving it a cruising speed adequate for its role as a cargo carrier. Its chief limitation is dive endurance. The vessel can sustain submerged operations for approximately twelve hours before it must surface to run its engines and replenish fuel. This is typically sufficient for transit between submerged habitats, underwater farms, and the factories and depots that many planets maintain on their ocean floors. Captains operating in coastal waters with elevated threat exposure will often surface to recharge in deeper water before making the final approach, accepting the operational delay to reduce risk.

Protection consists of a moderate layer of standard armor rated to BAR 7, sufficient to resist small arms fire and light weapons, but not designed to withstand sustained military attack. The Seahorse is not a combat vessel, and its armor reflects that reality.

Factory specifications include a pair of torpedo launcher mounts, one to each side, and a basic fire control package. In practice the vast majority of operating examples carry no torpedoes at all. The fire control equipment proved inadequate for reliable targeting, and most operators concluded the launchers consumed space and crew attention better spent elsewhere. The empty ports are left visible rather than plated over, functioning as a passive deterrent. A Seahorse running without weapons is the norm across the Inner Sphere; a fully armed example is the exception.

The Seahorse Cargo Sub is a small submersible cargo carrier designed to support underwater operations across the Inner Sphere and beyond. Produced by the Galtor Naval Yards on New Ivaarsen, the Seahorse has served as a workhorse of underwater commerce and logistics since the golden years of the First Star League. Simple to operate and widely available, the design has proven remarkably durable across centuries of use, surviving the upheavals of the Succession Wars with only modest updates to its basic configuration. The most current version of the vessel continues to be assembled on the construction slips at New Ivaarsen. Though it lacks the sophistication of more advanced submersibles, the Seahorse remains a practical and reliable choice for operators working in demanding undersea environments throughout the Inner Sphere.

The Seahorse is found most commonly in the hands of independent owner-operators and small planetary freight companies, typically serving routes between surface ports and submerged habitats, mining stations, or underwater industrial facilities. Larger corporations with extensive undersea extraction operations maintain fleets of the type to support logistical needs that surface vessels cannot reach. The design's modest cost and simple maintenance profile make it accessible to operators who cannot support more capable submersibles. The empty torpedo ports visible on most examples serve as the vessel's primary security measure, relying on the appearance of a threat-conscious crew rather than actual firepower.

The Seahorse traces its origins to the early Star League period, when the Galtor Naval Yards on New Ivaarsen developed it to meet growing demand for reliable underwater freight transport. From the outset the design prioritized simplicity and low cost over raw performance, making it accessible to independent operators and smaller planetary corporations that could not support more capable or specialized vessels. Production expanded steadily through the golden years of the Star League as planetary development pushed economic activity deeper underwater.

The collapse of the Star League and the onset of the Succession Wars changed the operating environment sharply. As piracy and freebooter raids spread across the Inner Sphere, even mundane cargo vessels became targets of opportunity. Responding to the threat, Galtor Naval Yards introduced torpedo launcher mounts on later production runs, fitting the Seahorse with paired torpedo installations and a basic fire control package. The intent was reasonable. The result was disappointing. Fire control proved inadequate for reliable targeting under operational conditions, and many captains reached the same conclusion independently. The launchers were more trouble than they were worth.

A practical norm developed among Seahorse operators over the following decades. Skippers stripped the weapons from their vessels, recovering space for additional cargo and fuel and reducing crew requirements at the same time. The empty weapon ports were left open and visible rather than plated over. A vessel with bare torpedo bays signals to potential raiders that someone installed weapons here once, and that the crew knows how to think about threats. Whether the deterrent effect holds up under scrutiny is debated, but the practice became so widespread that a fully armed Seahorse is now a curiosity. The unarmed version has become the de facto standard.

The most recent iteration of the design was produced through the Jihad period, incorporating accumulated operator preferences without formally abandoning the weapons capability. The Galtor Naval Yards' construction slips on New Ivaarsen remained active through multiple eras of political ownership. New Ivaarsen passed from Federated Suns control to Federated Commonwealth administration during the Renaissance period, returned briefly to Federated Suns jurisdiction during the Civil War and Jihad, and eventually came under Draconis Combine administration in the Dark Age, carrying the Seahorse production line with it.

The Silverfin is built on a 10.5-ton hydrofoil chassis constructed from a proprietary polymer composite blend, a material robust enough to endure repeated heavy-gale conditions without warping or snapping. When the foils are engaged, the 17-ton internal combustion engine drives the vessel to a flank speed of 120 km/h, making the Silverfin among the fastest naval support vehicles available to Inner Sphere wet navies. Three and a half tons of fuel gives it a range of over 2,000 km before refueling is required.

Primary armament is a single Magnum-Sperry Class 9 rotary machine gun designed for maritime use, mounted in the bow turret alongside two Sky Raven SRT-2 short-range torpedo launchers. Both weapon systems are linked to an Advanced Fire Control system, and together they are sufficient to engage pirate and smuggling craft. When Silverfins operate in coordinated groups, they can overwhelm better-armored targets with coordinated torpedo salvos.

The vessel's primary shortcoming is its armor. One ton of Windancer Lightwave commercial-grade protection carries a Barrier Armor Rating of 7, far below military-combat standards. A single full-powered shot from even a light military laser can penetrate the hull and require extensive repairs, though the hydrofoil frame itself remains structurally sound. The HUNTER communications suite is similarly fragile, as the combination of heavy vibration in hydrofoil mode and constant salt-spray exposure degrades its electronics and requires a complete overhaul every fifty years.

The Silverfin coastal cutter is a blue-water patrol hydrofoil produced by Windancer Marine Technologies of Terra, introduced in 2302. Designed by naval architect Tyler Raymonds and built in partnership with the Tadaki Company of Japan, the Silverfin was conceived in desperation and proved its worth in a single dramatic demonstration that saved its manufacturer from bankruptcy. The design quickly won contracts from every major government of the era, and Windancer spent the following centuries supplying Silverfin cutters to water-rich worlds across what would become the Inner Sphere.

The Silverfin is not a warship in the traditional sense. It serves as a tool of governance, patrolling coastlines and river routes, conducting anti-smuggling operations, and providing escort coverage for larger naval vessels. Its exceptional speed and range make it effective at those duties regardless of era, and the design's simplicity has allowed it to survive centuries of production with only minor revisions.

The Silverfin serves in coast guard and planetary militia naval forces across the Inner Sphere, assigned to patrol coastal approaches, police trade routes against smuggling, and escort larger naval vessels along important sea lanes. Nearly every water-rich world under any of the Great Houses has at least one Silverfin in service. The vessel's speed and endurance make it effective at rapid-response patrol work, and its straightforward maintenance requirements suit the limited resources of planetary militias.

In patrol pack formations, Silverfins compensate for their individual firepower limits. Coordinated torpedo salvos allow a group of Silverfins to engage armored naval vessels or even light BattleMechs wading coastal approaches, though such engagements are atypical. The vessel is not intended for sustained combat and relies on speed to disengage when facing military opposition.

The Silverfin's origins lie in the near-collapse of Windancer Marine Technologies in 2302. The company, facing imminent bankruptcy, committed every remaining asset to a new design by naval architect Tyler Raymonds. Raymonds proposed a hydrofoil frame using an advanced polymer composite for the foils, a material he believed could withstand conditions that would destroy conventional metal foil designs. Windancer partnered with the Tadaki Company, a Japanese venture capital firm, to fund a working prototype. Rather than a quiet sea trial, the company staged a spectacle: a two-day voyage directly into and out of a Class 3 typhoon in the Sea of Japan, broadcast widely to attract buyers. When the Silverfin returned with its foils intact, Windancer's future was secured overnight.

For the next several centuries, Windancer produced Silverfin cutters for all the major governments and Great Houses without significant alteration to the basic design. Torpedo launchers were added in 2423 to improve the vessel's anti-submarine capability. The only other recurring maintenance burden was the HUNTER communications suite, which required a complete overhaul every fifty years to address salt corrosion and vibration-induced component degradation. By the time of the Star League, virtually every water-rich world in the Inner Sphere had at least one Silverfin assigned to its coast guard or planetary militia fleet.

The Succession Wars disrupted Windancer's Terra-based production when Terra changed hands, but the design's broad licensing network meant Silverfins continued to be built across the Inner Sphere regardless of who controlled the original factory. The cutter's uncomplicated construction and minimal dependence on advanced components made it well suited to the technology contraction of that era, and loss of the Star League's manufacturing base affected the Silverfin far less than more sophisticated designs.

The White Tip is a 250-ton naval vessel designed around dual roles as a command platform and coastal combat asset. Its primary offensive capability comes from two Long Range Torpedo-15 launchers, one positioned forward and one aft, giving the vessel simultaneous coverage across both arcs. A Long Range Torpedo-10 rounds out the long-range battery, mounted in the turret alongside two Short Range Torpedo-4 launchers for close-range defense. An Extended Range Medium Laser in the bow provides a directed-energy option effective against surface targets and watercraft that may be resistant to torpedo fire.

The White Tip's armor is minimal by any military standard, relying on just four tons of civilian-grade material rated to BAR 8. This thin protection reflects the core design philosophy of avoidance over absorption. The vessel is intended to remain submerged and difficult to locate, not to absorb fire from dedicated combat units. A cruise speed of 3 and flank speed of 5 are unimpressive for its displacement, but underwater concealment compensates for what it lacks in straight-line performance.

Command facilities are substantial relative to the vessel's tonnage. Seven tons of communications equipment support a wide-spectrum communications capability, and the ship carries a MASH unit, medical quarters, and berthing for officers and support personnel. Advanced Fire Control guides the weapons suite. A 30-ton cargo hold allows extended independent deployment, reducing reliance on shore support during prolonged operations.

The White Tip command submarine was developed by Bigoti Seacraft on Keid in 3074, serving the Word of Blake Protectorate as a mobile command platform for aquatic operations. Rather than building to standard military specifications, Bigoti Seacraft drew on its experience in the civilian shipbuilding market, producing a vessel that met uprated civilian standards at a fraction of the cost of a true military design. This practical approach delivered a platform that could function both as a mobile headquarters and as an auxiliary combatant for coastal patrol work. The White Tip relied on its submersible capability to evade hostile forces rather than on heavy armor protection, a design philosophy that made it well-suited for contested aquatic environments. Despite its modest origins, the design proved resilient enough to outlast its original patron and eventually attract commercial interest well beyond the Protectorate.

The White Tip is deployed on worlds with significant aquatic terrain, where its submersible capability provides both a tactical and operational advantage. Operating as a mobile command platform, it is best suited to coordinating coastal and riverine operations from submerged positions that deny enemy forces an easy targeting solution. Long-range torpedo batteries allow engagement of surface and underwater targets at standoff distances, while the command facilities give embarked commanders the communications reach to direct dispersed forces across wide areas. The design's light protection means White Tip commanders favor submerged standoff tactics over surface engagements. Medical and personnel support facilities make extended independent deployments practical, allowing the vessel to serve as a self-sufficient mobile headquarters during prolonged coastal operations.

Bigoti Seacraft was a Keid-based company with deep roots in civilian maritime construction when the Word of Blake commissioned the White Tip in 3074. The Protectorate sought an affordable command platform for aquatic environments, and Bigoti's expertise in commercial vessel construction made them a natural choice. Rather than demanding military-specification systems throughout, the Blakists accepted a design built to enhanced civilian standards. This kept unit costs manageable while delivering the capabilities the Protectorate required: submersible operations, torpedo armament, and extensive command and communications facilities.

When Devlin Stone's Coalition forces arrived to liberate Keid, all six operational White Tips were deployed against the invaders. The submarines proved capable coastal defenders, using their submersible nature to strike and withdraw before Coalition forces could effectively respond. Despite the Protectorate's ultimate defeat, the performance of the White Tips was noted by Coalition commanders. The vessels demonstrated real utility as mobile command posts and coastal patrol assets, and Stone's forces committed resources to recovering and rebuilding four of the six submarines. The two destroyed in combat were beyond recovery.

The surviving White Tips were pressed into Coalition service, effectively transferring the design's operational legacy from the Word of Blake to what would become the Republic of the Sphere. Bigoti Seacraft, now operating under Republic governance on Keid, formalized this transition by beginning to market the White Tip to off-world customers by 3079. The design's low unit cost and proven submersible capability made it an attractive option for planetary militias and corporate security forces on aquatically active worlds.

In the ilClan era, Keid's ownership passed to the Capellan Confederation, bringing Bigoti Seacraft's production line under Capellan authority.
